stories.exam_facts: World Bank data cited in the article show that the share of firms exporting fell from 25% to 13% over roughly a decade, while frontier firms' share of export revenue rose from 37% to 69%, so exports are concentrated in fewer companies. The government wants to raise the SME share of GDP to 35% by 2030. Md Rubaiyath Sarwar, co-founder and managing director of Innovision Consulting, argues the MSME sector 'is designed as a sink to absorb youth whom we cannot employ in the formal sector' and says: 'We must stop this romanticism that a high number of MSMEs is good for Bangladesh. It is only good when the market has the appetite for it.' Niaz Asadullah, professor of economics at the University of Dhaka, said SMEs often absorb workers without the finance, technology, management capabilities or market access needed to raise output per worker, and that many remain small because expanding means more compliance-related expenses and greater exposure to tax uncertainty and demands from NBR officials. The article's lede cites Malaysia, where SMEs accounted for 14.7% of exports, 39.7% of GDP and 48.7% of employment in 2025, and Thailand, where SMEs accounted for 14.3% of exports during the first 10 months; the article cautions that international comparisons require care because countries define the sector in different ways.

stories.headline: “Choked by design”: How small, low bridges killing rivers in Bangladesh
stories.summary: A Prothom Alo investigation found small, low bridges built without regard for a river's life or navigability are choking Bangladesh's rivers. At Salehpur Bridge over the Turag, built by the Roads and Highways Department in 2023, approach roads encroach about 250 feet into the river and the bridge is only 59 paces long, so silt piles up upstream while the narrowed flow erodes the bed downstream; nobody keeps a complete record of such bridges, and the roads department, the disaster management ministry and local government share the blame.
stories.why_it_matters: The 250-foot encroachment and the 59-pace bridge are exact, quotable figures for BCS/Bank questions on rivers, environment and infrastructure — and the mechanism (approach roads extended into the channel to shorten a bridge) explains the next story about any dying river without re-studying it.
stories.exam_facts: BUET professor AKM Saiful Islam of the Institute of Water and Flood Management told Prothom Alo that narrowing a river causes two kinds of damage: silt gets trapped upstream and gradually fills the river, while water rushing through the narrowed section downstream erodes the riverbed and collapses the banks, and can effectively kill a river. Downstream of Salehpur Bridge the Turag widens again as it flows towards the Buriganga; houses and brick kilns have sprung up on land reclaimed from the river beside the bridge. Fisherman Kanu Mia of Salehpur village said: “Ever since the bridge was built, the river has become narrower. They have killed the river here with this bridge.” Culverts, like bridges, can also harm rivers and canals, and political influence is a factor in how these structures are built.
